# Generated Files Are Owned by the Build

> The CI plugin writes workflow files, so the question is who owns a file: the plugin or the developer. ZIO SBT gives two different answers, depending on the file.

## Files the Build Owns

`ci.yml`, `auto-approve.yml`, `auto-merge.yml` and the other generated workflows belong to `build.sbt`. Every one starts with an "autogenerated" header and is rewritten by `ciGenerateGithubWorkflow`. A hand edit is lost at the next generation, and `ciCheckGithubWorkflow` fails until the file matches what the build would write. This is deliberate: the build is the single source of truth, and a pull request that changes a workflow shows the change in `build.sbt` too.

The same applies to `.github/dependabot.yml`. When a feature is switched off, the plugin deletes only a file that carries its header, never a hand-written one.

## Files That Are Scaffolded Once

Two files are configuration of another tool and are expected to be edited by hand: `.github/release-drafter.yml` and `.scala-steward.conf`. The plugin writes them only the first time, when they do not exist. It never rewrites or deletes them afterward, and the drift check does not cover them.

## Why a Check Exists

A bot can change something that a generated file depends on, for example a Scala Steward bump of `zio-sbt-ci` itself. The committed files then no longer match what the build would write, and the `lint` job fails. The `regenerate-workflows.yml` workflow exists to fix exactly this on bot pull requests.

To keep the files in sync yourself, see [Keep the Generated Workflow in Sync](../how-to-guides/keep-the-workflow-in-sync.md).
